clue.text: Governesses en famille

blocks.note: surface reading: women employed to teach children in a household
setter's reading: women who govern within the family, its female heads

explanation.surface: A nanny-like teacher living with a family.
explanation.walkthrough: Governess suggests a hired tutor, but read literally it is a woman who governs, and en famille places her at the head of a family.
explanation.definitionFit: Matriarchs are women who rule a family or clan, literally governing it from the top.

clue.text: Main course sometimes follows the sweet

blocks.note: surface reading: the central dish of a dinner
setter's reading: the word that comes after sweet in a compound naming a confection

explanation.surface: A dinner where the main course comes after the pudding, oddly out of order.
explanation.walkthrough: At table the sweet follows this course, but in the word sweetmeat it comes after the sweet.
explanation.definitionFit: Flesh of an animal is the traditional principal dish of a dinner, served between starter and pudding.

clue.text: A number fit to be kept

definitions.note: an infinitive phrase standing for an adjective: able to be kept

blocks.note: ten is a number
fit in the sense of capable

explanation.surface: A figure judged suitable to keep on record.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that can be held or maintained, such as a position or argument, is described this way.

clue.text: Slip in dice, ta manipulation, that could cause a mutiny

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase standing for a noun: a thing that could cause a mutiny

indicators.note: manipulation means handling and working something over, so the preceding words are rearranged

blocks.note: as printed this word gives nothing; it is a misprint for 'in', taken as written
the letters of these three words taken together

explanation.surface: Sailors cheating at dice by palming loaded ones, the sort of thing that sets off a mutiny.
explanation.walkthrough: The page prints 'ta', which gives nothing; it must be a misprint for 'in', placed before the rearranged word for orderliness.
explanation.definitionFit: Lack of order and obedience among a crew is the breakdown that leads to revolt against officers.

clue.text: Thomas Hood did, in duplicate!

blocks.note: surface reading: something the poet Thomas Hood once did
setter's reading: his poem opens with the same verb said twice, 'I ..., I ...'

explanation.walkthrough: Thomas Hood's poem 'I Remember, I Remember' repeats its first phrase, so he did it twice over.
explanation.definitionFit: To recall something to mind is exactly what the poet's twice-repeated title says he does.

clue.text: These people seem backward to us

blocks.note: hind means at the back, rear
us taken as written, with to joining it on

explanation.surface: Some foreigners look old-fashioned from where we stand.
explanation.walkthrough: Backward looks like a judgement on the people, but it only supplies the word for rear.
explanation.definitionFit: The followers of the main religion of India are a people the clue points at generally.

clue.text: The ultimate in snobbery?

blocks.note: first meaning: the final one
second meaning: snob is an old word for a cobbler, and this is the cobbler's foot-shaped form

explanation.surface: Someone who is the very height of being a snob.
explanation.walkthrough: Snob once meant a shoemaker, so snobbery here is the cobbler's trade, not social pretension.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means final, and is also the wooden foot model a shoemaker shapes shoes around.

clue.text: Does it bring Lady Jan all out in a rash?

definitions.text: Does it bring Lady Jan all out in a rash?

blocks.note: surface reading: some titled woman breaking out after a misadventure
setter's reading: the body's reaction to something it cannot tolerate, producing spots

explanation.walkthrough: To bring someone out in a rash is the classic symptom of a sensitivity to food, pollen or the like.
explanation.definitionFit: An abnormal immune reaction to a substance often shows itself as hives or a skin eruption.

clue.text: He is not in his rightful place

definitions.text: He is not in his rightful place

blocks.note: surface reading: a man out of position or misplaced
setter's reading: a man on land where he has no right to be

explanation.definitionFit: Someone who enters private property without permission is literally somewhere he has no right to be.

clue.text: Initially used for date-bearing

blocks.note: setter's reading: the phrase is normally used only as its initials
surface reading: something stamped on things that carry a date, like coins

explanation.walkthrough: The Latin phrase for 'in the year of the Lord' usually appears as its initials AD beside a year.
explanation.definitionFit: This Latin expression marks years of the Christian era, abbreviated to two capitals on dates.

clue.text: Fruit is behind time, we hear

indicators.note: we hear points to sound rather than spelling, so the phrase is matched by its pronunciation

blocks.note: behind time means late or slow

explanation.surface: A crop that is ripening late in the season.
explanation.definitionFit: The small bitter blackthorn berry, used to flavour gin, is a kind of wild fruit.

clue.text: Galena yields the lead to him

definitions.text: Galena yields the lead to him

blocks.note: surface reading: someone let a person called Galena go in front
setter's reading: galena is the chief ore of lead, which gives up its metal to a specialist

explanation.walkthrough: Galena looks like a woman's name, but it is lead sulphide, the main ore from which lead is extracted.
explanation.definitionFit: A scientist who studies metals and extracts them from ores is the one an ore surrenders its lead to.

clue.text: Bird, half of which is round

blocks.note: surface reading: a bird partly of round shape
setter's reading: the bird's name split in halves, the second half spelling the clue's own little word

explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay is loose: the second half of the name spells 'is', and the first two letters turned round give BI, which hints at the double, 'bis'.
explanation.definitionFit: This long-billed wading bird, sacred in ancient Egypt, is a familiar crossword species.

clue.text: Play with a catchy theme

blocks.note: surface reading: a stage show whose tune is easy to remember
setter's reading: Agatha Christie's long-running London play, named for a device that catches rodents

explanation.walkthrough: Catchy here means built to catch, not memorable.
explanation.definitionFit: Agatha Christie's play has run in London's West End since 1952, and its title names a trap for small rodents.

clue.text: Great rendering of "The Sound of Music"

definitions.text: Great rendering of "The Sound of Music"

blocks.clueFragment: Great rendering of "The Sound of Music"
blocks.note: surface reading: a fine performance of the musical
setter's reading: the sound of music rendered at great volume

explanation.walkthrough: The musical's title is to be read literally as the sound music makes, and great as great loudness.
explanation.definitionFit: The Italian musical direction means very loudly, a marking for playing with the greatest force.

clue.text: Having singular partiality

blocks.note: surface reading: an unusual or peculiar fondness
setter's reading: singular as numerical, a single faction favoured

explanation.walkthrough: Singular suggests strange, but it means just one, and partiality is taking a part or faction.
explanation.definitionFit: Biased towards just one party in a dispute, so unfair and lacking balance.

clue.text: They may have been half-inclined to act the goat

definitions.text: They may have been half-inclined to act the goat

blocks.note: surface reading: people tempted to play the fool
setter's reading: creatures that are literally half goat in form

explanation.walkthrough: To act the goat is British slang for fooling about; these mythical woodland beings had goat legs and human upper bodies.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth, woodland companions of Dionysus were part man and part goat, and notoriously lustful.

clue.text: What's left to drink at the old Bull and Bush

blocks.clueFragment: What's left to drink at the old Bull and Bush
blocks.note: surface reading: whatever remains in the cellar of a famous pub
setter's reading: a fortified Portuguese tipple whose first part is the nautical word for left

explanation.walkthrough: The Old Bull and Bush is a Hampstead pub of music-hall song; left is the sailor's port side.
explanation.definitionFit: This sweet fortified Portuguese drink takes its name from the city of Oporto and shares it with the left side of a ship.

clue.text: Footballer's gear

blocks.note: surface reading: kit, equipment
setter's reading: the challenge a footballer makes to win the ball, which is also a word for equipment

explanation.definitionFit: The word means equipment, as in fishing gear, and also a footballer's challenge for the ball.

clue.text: Proverbially fair game

blocks.note: surface reading: a legitimate target
setter's reading: a sport whose name stands for fair play in the idiom that unfair conduct is 'not' it

explanation.walkthrough: 'It's not cricket' is a British idiom for unfair behaviour; the bat-and-ball game is thus the proverbial fair one.
explanation.definitionFit: The bat-and-ball sport is a byword for fair play, from the saying that cheating is not this game.

clue.text: Allowed, in a way, a game of chance

indicators.note: in tells us one word is placed inside the other that follows it

blocks.note: allowed, past tense of permit
a route is a way

explanation.surface: Gambling permitted, in some fashion, on a game of luck.
explanation.definitionFit: The casino wheel game, where a ball lands on a numbered slot, is a classic gamble.

clue.text: The dog to go wrong in a row

indicators.note: in means the preceding verb sits inside the word that follows

blocks.note: to err is to make a mistake
a tier is a row, as of seats

explanation.surface: A dog misbehaving in a line of animals.
explanation.definitionFit: A small breed originally used to dig out burrowing animals is a type of dog.

clue.text: He's bound to get the girl

definitions.text: He's bound to get the girl

blocks.note: surface reading: a man certain to win the woman, like a film hero
setter's reading: tied by a promise of marriage to the woman

explanation.walkthrough: Bound means committed by a pledge, not certain.
explanation.definitionFit: A man engaged to be married is pledged to wed his bride-to-be.

clue.text: It is scent processed by a boffin

indicators.note: processed means worked on and changed, so the letters before it are rearranged

blocks.note: the letters of these three words together

explanation.surface: A perfume developed in a laboratory by a researcher.
explanation.walkthrough: Boffin is British slang for a research scientist.
explanation.definitionFit: A boffin is an informal British term for a clever researcher in science or technology.

clue.text: Yet such steak is not uncommon

blocks.note: first meaning: steak cooked only briefly, still red inside
second meaning: seldom found, scarce

explanation.surface: A diner remarking that underdone steak is ordered all the time.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pretends the steak is common; 'not uncommon' is in fact a plain definition of the word.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means seldom found, and also describes meat cooked lightly and still red in the middle.

clue.text: Seers didn't necessarily depend on them

definitions.text: Seers didn't necessarily depend on them

blocks.note: surface reading: prophets who might rely on signs and portents
setter's reading: a burden or responsibility that falls on someone

explanation.walkthrough: The link is loose: the word splits as 'on us', and responsibility rests on whoever must bear it, which the seers need not.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a Latin term for a burden or duty resting on someone.

clue.text: Bedaubed state of Hamlet's cloak?

blocks.note: surface reading: smeared or stained condition
setter's reading: in Act 1 Hamlet describes his black mourning cloak with an adjective drawn from writing fluid

explanation.walkthrough: In Act 1 Hamlet calls his mourning garment his '... cloak, good mother', meaning it is black as the writing fluid.
explanation.definitionFit: Stained or as black as writing fluid, the epithet Shakespeare gives Hamlet's mourning garment.

clue.text: But it wasn't shown by the rude forefathers of Gray's hamlet

definitions.text: But it wasn't shown by the rude forefathers of Gray's hamlet

blocks.clueFragment: the rude forefathers of Gray's hamlet
blocks.note: surface reading: Gray's Elegy speaks of 'the rude forefathers of the hamlet', meaning simple rustic villagers
setter's reading: rude taken as uncouth, people who held nothing back

explanation.walkthrough: In Thomas Gray's Elegy rude means humble and unlearned; read as impolite, it describes people with no restraint.
explanation.definitionFit: Restraint holding back natural behaviour is what rude, unrestrained people fail to show.

clue.text: He take the part of Bot tom

indicators.note: taking a part of something means using only a portion of the following letters

blocks.note: the middle letters of the weaver's name from A Midsummer Night's Dream

explanation.surface: An actor cast as Bottom in Shakespeare's comedy.
explanation.walkthrough: Take the part of sounds like acting a role, but it means take a part of the name.
explanation.definitionFit: A man's name, so a male person, which He stands in for.

clue.text: Matters of interest of more than ordinary security

definitions.text: Matters of interest of more than ordinary security

blocks.note: surface reading: things worth paying attention to
setter's reading: interest-paying financial instruments secured above ordinary shares

explanation.walkthrough: Interest is money paid on a loan and security a financial bond, not attention and safety.
explanation.definitionFit: These are company loan bonds paying fixed interest, ranking ahead of ordinary shareholders for repayment.
